concept.name: Saga & Compensation Patterns

relationships.description: Sagas trade strong global isolation for availability.
Every saga step must tolerate retries.

reviewRecord.reviewNotes: Seeded for SPEC-062 pillar coverage matrix.

spark.summary: A Saga coordinates a multi-service business transaction as a sequence of local ACID transactions paired with compensating actions that semantically undo prior steps on failure, avoiding distributed 2-Phase Commit locks at the cost of eventual consistency.
spark.keyTakeaway: Design every saga step before the pivot transaction to be idempotent and paired with a compensating action, and persist state transitions via a transactional outbox so crashes never leave workflows orphaned.

concept.whyItMatters: Microservices with database-per-service cannot span a single ACID transaction across Order, Inventory, and Payment databases. Two-Phase Commit (XA/2PC) holds cross-network locks that stall throughput and block when a coordinator crashes. Sagas keep every local transaction fast and lock-free while guaranteeing either full completion or semantic rollback.
whenToUse: Multi-service workflows (e.g., e-commerce checkout, flight+hotel booking, loan origination) spanning independent databases.
Long-running business processes (seconds to days) involving external payment gateways or human approvals where DB locks cannot be held.
High-throughput systems where 2PC coordinator latency and lock contention would violate p99 SLOs.
whenNotToUse: Operations contained within a single database or monolith where a standard local ACID transaction is simpler and strictly isolated.
Hard real-time financial ledgers requiring strict serializability (zero dirty-read window) across partitions—use a NewSQL DB (Spanner/CockroachDB) instead.
Simple 2-step read-after-write flows where synchronous retry or a single outbox event suffices without compensation logic.
keyPoints: Every saga has three transaction classes: Compensable (undoable, e.g., ReserveInventory), Pivot (point of no return, e.g., ChargeCard), and Retriable (guaranteed to succeed, e.g., ConfirmOrder).
Orchestration (Temporal, AWS Step Functions) centralizes control flow and debugging, whereas Choreography (Kafka events) decouples services but hides global state.
Sagas provide ACD (Atomicity, Consistency, Durability) without Isolation—concurrent sagas can observe intermediate uncommitted states (dirty reads).
Countermeasures like Semantic Locks (PENDING_RESERVATION) and Commutative Updates prevent isolation anomalies without distributed locks.
The Transactional Outbox pattern (DB write + outbox row in one local ACID tx + Debezium CDC) prevents dual-write split-brain between DB commits and message brokers.

examples.title: E-Commerce Checkout Orchestration with Temporal
examples.scenario: A marketplace checkout spanned Order, Loyalty Points, Warehouse Inventory, and Stripe Payment; network timeouts frequently left loyalty points deducted on failed card charges.
examples.outcome: Modeling checkout as a Temporal Saga—with ReservePoints and ReserveStock as compensable steps before the ChargeStripe pivot—automatically refunded points and released stock within 400ms on payment declines.

examples.title: Preventing Overselling via Semantic Locks
examples.scenario: During a flash sale, a second customer's saga read stock=1 while the first customer's saga had not yet finalized payment, causing double-allocation.
examples.outcome: Introducing a Semantic Lock (status = PENDING_PAYMENT with a 10-minute TTL) on the inventory row blocked concurrent sagas from consuming reserved units until either ConfirmOrder or ReleaseStock ran.

tradeOffs.pro: Orchestration makes state, timeouts, and compensation order explicit in one workflow definition with clear observability.
tradeOffs.con: Adds an orchestrator dependency (Temporal/Step Functions) that must be operated and scaled alongside microservices.

tradeOffs.pro: Zero cross-service locks; individual services remain available and fast even if downstream peers are slow.
tradeOffs.con: Requires writing custom compensating logic and handling dirty-read isolation anomalies.

tradeOffs.pro: Semantic locks (PENDING states) prevent conflicting sagas from acting on transient intermediate data.
tradeOffs.con: Adds state-machine complexity and requires TTL sweepers to reap abandoned locks.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain
failureModes.description: A service commits its local DB transaction but crashes before publishing the Kafka/SQS event, stalling the saga indefinitely.
failureModes.mitigation: Use the Transactional Outbox pattern: write the domain change and outbox event in the same local ACID transaction, then tail it via Debezium CDC or a poller.

failureModes.name: Non-Idempotent Compensation
failureModes.description: A network timeout triggers a retry of RefundPayment or ReleaseStock, crediting the customer twice or inflating inventory count.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a deterministic idempotency key (saga_id + step_name) to every forward and compensating command, enforced via a UNIQUE constraint.

failureModes.name: Failing Compensating Transaction
failureModes.description: After ChargeCard fails, the compensating ReleaseStock call also fails due to a DB outage, leaving inventory permanently locked.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat all compensating actions as retriable: retry with exponential backoff + jitter, route poison pills to a DLQ, and alert an operator for manual reconciliation.

failureModes.name: Missing Isolation (Lost Update / Dirty Read)
failureModes.description: A concurrent saga reads or overwrites a record modified by an in-flight saga that later rolls back, acting on phantom state.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply semantic locks (status flags), commutative updates (delta +/- instead of absolute set), or versioned optimistic concurrency checks.

commonMistakes: Placing a non-compensable side effect (like sending an email or shipping webhook) before the pivot transaction.
Assuming compensating transactions never fail and omitting retries or Dead-Letter Queues for rollback paths.
Building Choreography sagas across >4 services without a correlation_id, making production failures impossible to trace.
Skipping idempotency keys on forward and backward steps, causing duplicate charges or double refunds on at-least-once delivery.
Forgetting to set saga step timeouts, allowing stuck workflows to hold semantic inventory locks forever.

sections.content:
## The idea

In a distributed architecture where each service owns its database, a single business operation (like placing an order) cannot rely on a traditional ACID transaction across services. Holding Two-Phase Commit (2PC) locks over WAN/RPC boundaries destroys throughput and halts the system whenever a participant hangs.

A **Saga** breaks a distributed transaction $T$ into a sequence of local ACID transactions $T_1, T_2, \dots, T_n$. If step $T_k$ fails, the saga executes compensating transactions $C_{k-1}, \dots, C_1$ in reverse order to semantically undo the prior effects (e.g., issuing a refund or releasing reserved stock).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an e-commerce checkout managed by an **Orchestrator** (e.g., Temporal):

1. **T1 (Compensable) — Create Order**: Order Service inserts an order row with `status = PENDING` and an outbox record in one local PostgreSQL transaction.
2. **T2 (Compensable) — Reserve Stock**: Inventory Service decrements `available_qty` and inserts a semantic lock `reservation(order_id, TTL=10m)`.
3. **T3 (Pivot) — Charge Card**: Payment Service calls Stripe with `Idempotency-Key: pay_{order_id}`. Stripe returns `402 Card Declined`.
4. **Pivot Failure -> Compensate**: Because `T3` failed, the orchestrator reverses direction and invokes `C2` (`ReleaseStock(order_id)`) and `C1` (`CancelOrder(order_id, reason='PAYMENT_DECLINED')`).
5. **Idempotent Convergence**: Even if `C2` times out once and is retried, the `reservations` table checks `order_id` status and applies the release exactly once.

sections.content:
## Handling missing isolation (ACD vs ACID)

Because local transactions commit immediately, Sagas lack **Isolation**. A concurrent request can read uncommitted business state (e.g., an order marked `PENDING` or stock temporarily deducted). To prevent anomalies without distributed locks:

- **Semantic Lock**: Mark records with `status = PENDING_RESERVATION` so other sagas either block or reject edits until the lock clears.
- **Commutative Updates**: Express mutations as deltas (`balance += -50`) rather than absolute overwrites (`balance = 150`), so out-of-order compensations still converge.
- **Pessimistic View**: Reorder steps so high-risk checks (fraud/credit) run before low-risk reservations, and put customer notifications strictly after the pivot.

## Distributed transaction patterns compared

| Pattern | Isolation | Throughput / Latency | Coupling & Complexity | Best Use Case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **2PC / XA** | Full ACID | Low (cross-network locks) | Tight; coordinator single point of stall | Legacy single-datacenter XA resources |
| **Orchestration Saga** | ACD (needs countermeasures) | High (local locks only) | Explicit central workflow; easy debugging | Complex 3+ step workflows (Temporal, Step Functions) |
| **Choreography Saga** | ACD (needs countermeasures) | High (async pub/sub) | Low coupling, hard to trace global state | Simple 2-3 service event-driven flows |
| **Transactional Outbox** | Local ACID + At-Least-Once | Very High | Minimal; requires CDC or poller | Reliable event emission without dual-write bugs |

## Failure modes

- **Stuck Semantic Locks**: If an orchestrator or consumer crashes mid-saga without recovery, `PENDING` reservations can lock inventory indefinitely. Always attach a TTL sweeper or workflow timeout.
- **Out-of-Order Event Delivery**: In Choreography sagas over partitioned topics, a `CancelOrder` event can arrive before `CreateOrder` if partition keys differ. Partition strictly by `saga_id` / `aggregate_id`.
- **Partial Pivot Ambiguity**: A timeout on `ChargeCard` leaves the outcome unknown—never compensate immediately without first querying the payment provider's status endpoint using the `Idempotency-Key`.

## Transactional outbox and idempotency

Reliable sagas depend on **at-least-once** delivery paired with **idempotent** receivers:

- Store an `inbox` / `processed_events(event_id PRIMARY KEY)` table in each participant's database and check/insert it inside the same local transaction as the business update.
- Use **Debezium CDC** or a transactional outbox table so database commits and event publications are atomic.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Classify every step as Compensable, Pivot, or Retriable; keep non-undoable actions (emails, webhooks) strictly after the Pivot.
- [ ] Persist saga state and outbox events in a single local ACID transaction (no dual writes).
- [ ] Require deterministic idempotency keys (`saga_id + step`) on all forward and compensating endpoints.
- [ ] Protect in-flight entities with Semantic Locks (`PENDING_*`) and TTL expiration sweepers.
- [ ] Configure exponential backoff + jitter and a Dead-Letter Queue for compensating transactions.
- [ ] Propagate `saga_id` and `traceparent` across all RPCs and broker headers.

interviewProblems.title: Saga & Compensation Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Saga & Compensation Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Saga And Compensation Patterns

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A Saga coordinates a multi-service business transaction as a sequence of local ACID transactions paired with compensating actions that semantically undo prior steps on failure, avoiding distributed 2-Phase Commit locks at the cost of eventual consistency.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Inventory Service applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Payment Service.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Payment Service experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use the Transactional Outbox pattern: write the domain change and outbox event in the same local ACID transaction, then tail it via Debezium CDC or a poller.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Design every saga step before the pivot transaction to be idempotent and paired with a compensating action, and persist state transitions via a transactional outbox so crashes never leave workflows orphaned.
Avoid trap: Placing a non-compensable side effect (like sending an email or shipping webhook) before the pivot transaction.
Avoid trap: Assuming compensating transactions never fail and omitting retries or Dead-Letter Queues for rollback paths.
When to reach for it: Multi-service workflows (e.g., e-commerce checkout, flight+hotel booking, loan origination) spanning independent databases.
When to reach for it: Long-running business processes (seconds to days) involving external payment gateways or human approvals where DB locks cannot be held.

putItTogether.title: Putting Saga And Compensation Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Design every saga step before the pivot transaction to be idempotent and paired with a compensating action, and persist state transitions via a transactional outbox so crashes never leave workflows orphaned.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Saga And Compensation Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Modeling checkout as a Temporal Saga—with ReservePoints and ReserveStock as compensable steps before the ChargeStripe pivot—automatically refunded points and released stock within 400ms on payment declines.
